title: Piercing the skies above Paranal
caption: Laser beams from Unit Telescope 4, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Framed against the star-filled sky of Paranal, UT4, one of the four 8-m telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope, pierces the night with four laser beams from inside its dome.

The lasers come from the 4 Laser Guide Star Facility, which UT4 uses to make its own artificial stars. The beams excite sodium atoms about 90 km above the ground, making them glow. The telescope studies how these guide stars are smeared by the atmosphere, the same turbulence that makes stars twinkle, and works out how to compensate.

The corrections are carried out by UT4's adaptive optics system, which precisely reshapes the telescope's secondary mirror to cancel the atmospheric disturbances it measures. With adaptive optics, a telescope on the ground can take far sharper images than the air would normally allow, nearly as good as sending the VLT into space.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph at ESO's Paranal Observatory, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, making the laser beams and faint stars more prominent than they would appear to someone standing there.

explore: The other three 8-m telescopes are due to get one laser each, as part of upgrades to the VLT Interferometer and its GRAVITY+ instrument, which combines light from several telescopes into a huge 'virtual' telescope.
ESO's Extremely Large Telescope, being built not far from Paranal, will have at least 6 lasers.
